claims.text: The as-synthesized (MnNiSi)0.62(FeCoGe)0.38 alloy has a high caloric response under applied field and pressure.
The as-synthesized alloy has poor mechanical integrity and tends to crack.
The cracking is caused by a continuous, inherently brittle intermetallic phase.
Rapid solution treatment followed by moderate-temperature annealing will invert the continuous brittle phase into a continuous ductile matrix containing dispersed precipitates.
A rapid quench after solution treatment will freeze the relevant high-temperature state.
The load-bearing matrix produced by the treatment will likely be a disordered BCC or FCC phase.
The original caloric phase will form fine, uniformly distributed precipitates in the ductile matrix.
Phase separation into fine precipitates will interrupt crack propagation.
A continuous ductile matrix will improve load transfer, toughness, and mechanical integrity.
The ductile matrix will retain the field-induced phase-change capability required for the caloric effect.
The caloric mechanism will remain active in the dispersed precipitates despite the microstructural rearrangement.
The treatment will increase compressive and tensile strength beyond the levels achieved by the epoxy and indium composite routes.
The treated alloy will attain a strength above 220 MPa.
The treatment will reduce cracking relative to the untreated alloy.
The treated alloy will retain its applied-field and pressure-induced caloric response within 10% of the untreated alloy.
Epoxy-containing Mn0.98CoGe previously achieved compressive strengths of 152–218 MPa.
Indium composites previously achieved only 48 MPa compressive strength while improving heat transport.
Excessive annealing temperature or duration could cause phase coarsening or alter the caloric transformation temperatures.
The proposed microstructure will remain effective from ambient to moderately elevated temperatures under the same field and pressure conditions used for the untreated alloy.
A failure to achieve the specified mechanical improvement while retaining caloric response within 10% would falsify the hypothesis.

contradictions.description: The caloric phase is identified as the dispersed precipitate phase, but the mechanism also says that the ductile matrix retains the field-induced phase-change capability. This leaves the location of the active caloric transformation internally inconsistent.

The predicted strength target is >220 MPa, whereas the falsification rule asks for at least a 10% increase over an unspecified epoxy specimen. If the 218 MPa epoxy result is used, the latter threshold is about 240 MPa, so a result satisfying the stated target could still be declared a failure.
